subject: Issue with ds() function detecting the observations

messages.author: e183a94721e02db4
messages.subject: Issue with ds() function detecting the observations
parts:
Hi all, 

I am using 'Distance' in R and the models I am running are having issues recognising the number of observations in the data frame. It is only recognising 1 observation... I am really not sure what the issue is.. Maybe something with my .csv file?


I have attached the data and provided some code to run it below. 

Are there any obvious issues with the df? 



library(Distance) 

grig_data <-read.csv('green_ig_data_2020.csv',header=T, sep=',') 


# check data frames
summary(grig_data) 
str(grig_data) 



#function for helping with unit conversions for extrapolation 
unit_conversion<-convert_units("Metre", NULL, "Hectare")


# baseline model - half-normal detection function, no adjustments, no covariates, no truncation.
hn0 <- ds(grig_data,
          truncation =  ,
          formula = ~ 1,
          transect = "point",
          key = "hn",
          adjustment = NULL,
          convert.units = unit_conversion)


summary(hn0)  


I get the Warning message:

1: in qt(ci.width, estimate.table$df): NaNs produced

 

The top of the summary looks like:

Summary for distance analysis

Number of observations :  1

Distance range         :  0  -  280


If anyone can spot the problem, please help.

Kind regards,
Vaughn Bodden

messages.author: 7482eee8d2863d12
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Issue with ds() function detecting the observations
parts:
Hmm - worked fine for me (attached code), although I had to remove
column 21 from the dataset in the call to ds() because "observer" is a
reserved word and I got an error message with it in. If the same code
produces different results on different machines then it's often hard to
diagnose -- but I'd start by checking carefully that the data frame in
by read.csv is exactly as you think it should be.

(I notice from the plot and gof test that the baseline hn model gave a
poor fit, with too many observations close to the point relative to what
is expected by the fitted model. Not necessarily indicative of a
problem, since this is just a baseline model, but you may find a model
that fits well (and after truncation, etc) has quite a steep drop-off in
detectability at relatively small ranges, so you'll need to ask yourself
if this is plausible or whether there could be some problem such as
animal movement.)

Cheers, Len

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Issue with ds() function detecting the observations
parts:
It seems to work when I rename the the observer column. 
I updated my Distance library version from 1.0.0 to 1.0.1, ran the code without changing the column name, and I got the error message about 'observer' being a reserved name.  I didn't get it using the previous version.

Thanks for the pointers! There are also 50 points we repeated that were not included in the data I sent over. I am going to include those and account for the extra effort. 
But even with all of the detections in the model, the detection function is still skewed and the fit isn't the best.  See the figures attached.

This data is from a island wide survey for Green Iguanas in the Caribbean. The animals are invasive here and do well in urban/ suburban areas. So we end up using roadways for a lot of our survey points which is likely causing the spike at close range. I know this type of bias can be large, especially for reptiles, but access issues would make it hard to do the survey without using the roads. 

Thank for your help.

Kind regards,
Vaughn

messages.author: 9dce01a6123da978
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Issue with ds() function detecting the observations
parts:
Just a thought Vaughn, but if off-road transects aren't a realistic option and you reckon that sampling routes following roads are resulting in a highly non-random distance distribution of these beasts, you might consider using the road transect counts as an index of abundance, rather than trying to convert them into actual densities. If there is a reason you need the real densities then this isn't a good option. But often people decide they need densities in situations where relative abundances might serve them just as well. For instance, if your main purpose is to compare between islands, habitats, towns etc. to identify where problems with these iguanas are worst, a good measure of relative abundance could work just as well as true densities.

If for any reason you really need true densities, you might try short transects going perpendicular to the road, to get a sense of the degree to which lizard distribution is skewed towards the road. The feasibility of this would obviously depend on your finding an adequate number of sufficiently representative points along your roads where it is possible to run perpendicular transects that are long enough to pick up the relevant variation in iguana density with distance from road.

Whatever you do, I imagine road type (width and surface) might be an important thing to control for in your analyses. 

Cheers,

Mark

messages.author: e183a94721e02db4
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Issue with ds() function detecting the observations
parts:
Hi Mark,

Thanks for your suggestions! 

I am revisiting your comment because, again, I am designing a survey for an iguana on a different island (the native species on Cayman Brac, Cayman Islands) where accessibility to habitat is very limited and roads are practically necessary to move through the jagged karst terrain. 

I have attached a few images of the survey area habitat and the target species if that helps paint the picture.  There is a huge bluff (i.e. cliff) the runs down the center of the island that has 200 - 500 meters of low lying areas flanking either side of it on the coast. The coastal areas are where most of the iguanas are seen and where habitat is more accessible.   


Do you (or any on the group list) think that stratifying the density estimates by off-road and within a certain distance to the road (e.g. based on home range sizes of animals that may be attracted to the road) is a viable way to account for road bias for iguanas attracted to the roads? Still, the challenge will be not having enough replicates of off-road transects, likely leading to poor estimate for that region. But at least it will be more representative of the survey design. 

I have read Marques et. al. (2013) on using independent location information to account for density gradients in line transects but I don't think I can implement the models described. 

As a second option, I'm leaning more towards your previous suggestion; to use transects perpendicular to the road in these coastal areas where possible and then use a mix of mostly on-road or on-trail transects on the interior bluff. At least on the coast, we will be able to get a sense of how attracted the iguanas are to the road and a more precise estimate. 

Any comments or suggestions would be appreciated.  

All the best,

Vaughn

Do you (or any on the group list) think that stratifying the density estimates by off-road and within a certain distance to the road (e.g. based on home range sizes of animals that may be attracted to the road) is a viable way to account for road bias for iguanas attracted to the roads? Still, the challenge will be not having enough replicates of off-road transects, likely leading to poor estimate for that region. But at least it will be more representative of the survey design. 

I have read Marques et. al. (2013) on using independent location information to account for density gradients in line transects but I don't think I can implement the models described. 

As a second option, I'm leaning more towards your previous suggestion; to use transects perpendicular to the road in these coastal areas where possible and then use a mix of mostly on-road or on-trail transects on the interior bluff. At least on the coast, we will be able to get a sense of how attracted the iguanas are to the road and a more precise estimate. 

Any comments or suggestions would be appreciated.  

All the best,

Vaughn

Hi Vaughn,

So there is a road up on the bluff, too? I think your best course of action probably depends on survey effort available to you, but it sounds like you are aware of all the relevant issues and potential sources of bias. If I am understanding this system and your species correctly, then you might hope that densities of lizards off-road are relatively low. Then you could do a mix of (relatively straightforward and quick) road transects (probably restricting sampling area to the road itself, and assuming detection rate close to 1) and perpendicular transects for off-road habitat, the latter stratified by distance to road, as you suggest. If off-road densities are relatively low then wide confidence limit on estimates from these might not be so important. Ideally, you might find that off-road densities are predicted by on-road densities in the same perpendicular transects. That might allow you to get at reasonable estimates sticking largely to road surveys.

Great photos by the way! And best of luck with your study! 

Mark

Vaughn

A challenging problem when it comes to estimating abundance of a critically endangered species.  By definition, endangered species are rare.

Your aim should be to produce a defensible estimate.  You have discussed some of the threats to the estimate from your proposed survey.  Attempt to minimise those threats, which will likely entail more challenging field work.  A premise of design-based sampling inference is that places you survey are representative of places you do not survey.  A corollary is that if some portions of the island have zero probability of being sampled, you should not make inference about those portions of the island.

As the investigator, you choose the compromise between strength of your inference and the effort you are able to expend.

Thanks for all of your comments, Mark and Eric. 

It is a challenging system. Securing enough detections is also a concern. This species also occurs on another island, in greater abundance, where we have surveyed successfully for a few years but the design has similar issues with accessibility so lessons learnt will be applied there too.  

We are planning to conduct a pilot survey in areas where iguanas are known to occur to get a sense of the amount of effort that might be needed in the ideal case. We may also compare road-biased transects to ones perpendicular to road in accessible areas to compare encounter rates, densities, etc.  The pilot survey will hopefully clarify some of the issues and what types of inferences will be practical for this population.  

The photo of the iguana was taken by John Binns.   

All the best,
Vaughn Bodden
